children: US Senator Marsha Blackburn has taken the rare step as a Republican lawmaker of blocking one of US President Donald Trump's judicial nominees, at least for now, by withholding support for a White House lawyer nominated to serve on the bench in her home state.

Samuel Adkisson, who serves in the White House Counsel's Office as an associate counsel, had been expected to appear before the Senate Judiciary Committee on Wednesday in connection with his nomination last month by Trump to become a judge on the US District Court for the Eastern District of Tennessee.

But the panel did not take up Adkisson's nomination after Blackburn, a member of the committee who is running to be Tennessee's governor, did not return a so-called "blue slip" supporting his nomination, according to a committee aide.

Senators must return blue slips, named for the color of the forms, ​to the Senate Judiciary Committee in order for district court judge nominees from their home states ⁠to be considered, giving the senators leverage over who the White House picks.

It was unclear why Blackburn, who was not at Wednesday's hearing, did not submit a blue slip supporting Adkisson, who previously worked under Senator Chuck Grassley in his role as the panel's chairman during US Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh's 2018 confirmation hearing.
Spokespeople for Blackburn did not respond to requests for comment.
White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis in a statement called Adkisson "one of the brightest young conservative lawyers in the country" and said he would make an "outstanding judge."

In nominating Adkisson, Trump in a social media post last month credited him for his work on "numerous important cases," highlighting his work in particular on Trump v. Slaughter, in which the high court in June said the president had broad authority to fire regulatory agency heads.

Tennessee's other Republican senator, Bill Hagerty, had at the time of Adkisson's nomination hailed the choice, noting he had previously also served as a law clerk to Supreme Court Chief Justice John Roberts. Blackburn did not comment publicly on the nomination.

Mike Davis, a Trump ally who runs the conservative group the Article III Project, in a post on X late Tuesday called Blackburn's decision to block Adkisson a "stunning development" and a "grave mistake."
"We could not get a more brilliant, conservative, bold, and fearless pick for the federal bench," Davis wrote.

Adkisson was not the only nominee to be absent from Wednesday's hearing, the last scheduled on judicial nominees before the November 2 midterm elections in which Democrats hope to reclaim control of the Republican-led Senate.

Grassley kicked the session off by saying that due to delays in getting background investigation paperwork from the FBI, Brad Kelley, a partner at law firm Littler Mendelson, nominated to a judgeship in the Eastern District of Louisiana, would also not be considered at the meeting.
"This was a delay in getting paperwork from the FBI, and I’m confident that Mr. Kelley will sit for our next hearing," Grassley said.
